(function() { 'use strict'; class AIEthicsAdapter extends USF.SimulationAdapter { constructor() { super(); this.name = 'AI Ethics & Responsible Governance'; this.version = '1.1.0'; this.ROUNDS = [ { titleKey: 'round1_title', title: 'Round 1: The Governance Inventory', description: 'Week 1 as CAIGO: Your AI portfolio audit is complete. Grupo Iberia Financiero has 23 production AI models, of which 7 qualify as High-Risk under the EU AI Act. Only 2 have partial conformity assessments. None have formal technical documentation meeting EU AI Act standards.

Critical findings:
- The loan approval model (7 years old) shows self-employed applicants approved at 22 points lower than salaried applicants with similar profiles.
- The HR screening model was trained on data where successful hires were 73% male and 82% without career gaps.
- The fraud detection model (saving €28M/year) flags 12 postal codes with high immigrant populations at 3.4x the rate of other areas.

Your task: Choose 3 of 5 governance initiatives for your 90-day priority plan. Budget and staff are limited.', context: 'EU AI Act deadline: August 2026 (full compliance required)
Board mandate: Regulatory compliance + proactive governance
Team: 4 staff members, €800K annual governance budget
Political reality: Business unit leaders believe AI drives their best performance metrics', options: [ 'A: Full conformity assessment for all 7 high-risk models + Loan model emergency audit + AI ethics training', 'B: Loan model emergency audit + Public AI Transparency Report + AI ethics training for tech staff', 'C: Full conformity assessment for all 7 high-risk models + HR model third-party audit + Transparency Report', 'D: Loan model emergency audit + HR model third-party audit + Public AI Transparency Report', 'E: Full conformity assessment only for all 7 high-risk models (focus all resources)' ], optimalChoice: 3, scores: { regulatory: [-15, -8, -18, -12, -20], trust: [5, 12, 10, 15, 2], business: [-8, -3, -10, -5, -12], maturity: [0.4, 0.5, 0.5, 0.6, 0.3] }, feedback: [ 'Solid regulatory focus, but the lack of a public transparency commitment leaves stakeholder trust underaddressed. Ethics training alone is slow to build maturity.', 'Good balance of substantive action (loan audit), public accountability (transparency report), and capability building (training). This reflects a multi-dimensional governance theory.', 'Strong on regulatory compliance and substantive audits, but the resource strain of simultaneous full assessment and two audits may cause execution failures.', 'Excellent portfolio approach: substantive action on the two highest-risk models, combined with transparency to build credibility. This signals both urgency and accountability.', 'Pure compliance focus. While addressing the EU AI Act deadline, this ignores the immediate human harm from biased models and misses the trust-building opportunity.' ] }, { titleKey: 'round2_title', title: 'Round 2: The Fraud Detection Dilemma', description: 'Week 6: The Immigrant Community Association of Catalonia (AIC) has sent a letter to the CEO alleging that the fraud detection system is profiling immigrant communities. The letter has been copied to AESIA (the Spanish AI supervisory authority). It is not yet public.

The fraud team is defensive: the model prevents €28M in annual losses and is technically accurate overall.', context: 'Technical facts: The model uses 47 features. Postal code is not a direct feature, but proxy variables (account tenure by area, payment network density, balance volatility) correlate strongly with postal code and implicitly with immigrant community concentration.

Disparity data: Overall false positive rate is 2.1% (industry benchmark: 3.5%). But in the 12 flagged postal codes, the false positive rate is 7.8% \u2014 innocent customers there are flagged at nearly 4x the rate.

Cost of each false positive: Average 3 hours for customer resolution; 12% affect time-sensitive payments (rent, utilities, medical).

Model redesign cost: Removing proxy features reduces accuracy by ~8%, increasing fraud losses by ~€2.2M/year. Fairness-aware ML techniques could reduce the disparity while limiting accuracy loss.', options: [ 'A: Reject the allegation; defend the model as accurate and non-discriminatory; no changes', 'B: Acknowledge disparate impact; commit to independent audit; suspend model in flagged postal codes pending results', 'C: Acknowledge disparate impact; accept €2.2M cost to remove proxy features; redesign model; engage AIC in dialogue', 'D: Acknowledge disparate impact; redesign using fairness-aware ML to reduce disparity without full €2.2M loss; engage AIC and AESIA proactively', 'E: Refer entirely to Legal; take no public position until legal review is complete' ], optimalChoice: 3, scores: { regulatory: [10, -5, -10, -12, 3], trust: [-15, 5, 12, 15, -8], business: [0, -10, -8, -4, 0], maturity: [-0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.6, 0.0] }, feedback: [ 'Legally dangerous: the disparate impact evidence is documented and AESIA is already involved. Denial invites enforcement action and reputational crisis.', 'Acknowledging the issue is right, but suspending the model entirely in those areas creates operational disruption and leaves fraud risk unmanaged.', 'Ethically principled, but accepting the full cost without exploring fairness-aware alternatives overstates the trade-off. The Pareto frontier between fairness and accuracy has not been explored.', 'Advanced responsible AI practice: fairness-aware techniques (adversarial debiasing, threshold optimization) can reduce disparate impact while preserving significant accuracy. Proactive engagement with both AIC and AESIA builds trust and reduces regulatory risk.', 'Deferring to Legal without a governance position is diffusion of responsibility \u2014 precisely the failure mode the CAIGO role exists to prevent.' ] }, { titleKey: 'round3_title', title: 'Round 3: The Loan Approval Audit Results', description: 'Month 3: The independent audit of the loan approval model reveals results worse than expected.

Key findings:
- Self-employed applicants with equivalent financial profiles are approved at 24 percentage points lower than salaried applicants.
- Historical default rates for approved self-employed applicants are actually 0.3 points lower than salaried ones \u2014 the bias has no actuarial justification.
- The model was trained on 2016-2019 data reflecting an undocumented credit officer preference against self-employment.
- Approximately 4,200 applications per year may have been unfairly denied over 4 years.
- Estimated credit capacity denied: €840M with downstream effects on housing, small business, and family finances.', context: 'Legal exposure: Potential class action liability, CNMV regulatory action, and AESIA enforcement.
The core question: What does the organization owe to the ~16,800 people who may have been unfairly denied credit over 4 years?
Board sentiment: Deep reluctance toward public disclosure due to litigation risk.
Regulatory reality: Self-disclosure to regulators generally results in significantly reduced penalties.', options: [ 'A: Remediate the model immediately; accept future applications under corrected model; no disclosure of past decisions', 'B: Remediate model; proactively contact affected applicants from past 4 years and offer re-evaluation', 'C: Remediate model; contact affected applicants; establish redress fund; publicly disclose through press release', 'D: Remediate model; engage court-supervised settlement to determine redress; disclose to regulators but not publicly pending settlement', 'E: Pause all loan processing pending full review of entire model portfolio' ], optimalChoice: 2, scores: { regulatory: [-3, -8, -15, -12, -5], trust: [-5, 8, 18, 10, -3], business: [0, -5, -10, -7, -18], maturity: [0.1, 0.4, 0.7, 0.5, 0.2] }, feedback: [ 'Fixing the future while hiding the past is legally dangerous \u2014 failure to disclose a material compliance issue may constitute fraud by omission. Regulators will view this harshly if discovered independently.', 'Proactive outreach to affected applicants demonstrates genuine accountability. However, without a structured redress mechanism, re-evaluation alone may be insufficient for applicants who suffered downstream harm.', 'The most ethically principled and strategically strongest long-term choice. Self-disclosure reduces regulatory penalties, and proactive accountability builds durable institutional trust. The board will resist, but the CAIGO role exists precisely for this kind of governance courage.', 'Sophisticated legal strategy combined with ethical seriousness. Court supervision provides structure but delays accountability. Regulators appreciate disclosure even if public communication is deferred.', 'Operationally destructive. Pausing all lending over one model punishes current applicants for past governance failures and signals organizational panic rather than competence.' ] }, { titleKey: 'round4_title', title: 'Round 4: The Governance Architecture', description: 'Month 3: You must present the AI Governance Framework to the Board Risk Committee. Four committee members have different priorities:

- Compliance Director: Wants regulatory adherence above all.
- CTO: Wants governance embedded in development, not imposed by committees.
- External Director: Former NGO leader; wants genuine stakeholder representation.
- CFO: Wants governance that demonstrably creates business value.

Your task: Select the governance architecture that best balances all perspectives. Budget allows up to 8 of 12 possible components.', context: 'Available components (each option below selects 8):

1. Board AI Ethics Committee (external experts)
2. AI Risk Management System (ISO 42001 aligned)
3. AI Impact Assessment process (mandatory pre-deployment)
4. Algorithmic Fairness Testing toolkit
5. Explainability layer on consumer-facing decisions (SHAP-based)
6. AI Incident Response Protocol
7. Employee AI Ethics Speak-Up Channel
8. External Stakeholder Advisory Panel
9. Annual AI Transparency Report
10. AI Developer Certification Program
11. AI Commercial Opportunity Register
12. Continuous Model Monitoring System', options: [ 'A: Components 1,2,3,4,5,6,9,10 (Compliance-heavy: ethics committee, risk system, impact assessment, fairness testing, explainability, incident response, transparency report, developer certification)', 'B: Components 2,3,4,6,7,9,11,12 (Operational: risk system, impact assessment, fairness testing, incident response, speak-up channel, transparency report, commercial register, continuous monitoring)', 'C: Components 1,2,3,5,7,8,9,12 (Balanced: ethics committee, risk system, impact assessment, explainability, speak-up channel, stakeholder panel, transparency report, continuous monitoring)', 'D: Components 2,4,6,7,9,10,11,12 (Innovation-enabling: risk system, fairness testing, incident response, speak-up channel, transparency report, developer certification, commercial register, continuous monitoring)', 'E: Components 1,3,5,8,9,10,11,12 (Stakeholder-focused: ethics committee, impact assessment, explainability, stakeholder panel, transparency report, developer certification, commercial register, continuous monitoring)' ], optimalChoice: 2, scores: { regulatory: [-8, -10, -12, -7, -6], trust: [6, 8, 14, 7, 10], business: [-6, -2, -3, 0, -1], maturity: [0.5, 0.6, 0.8, 0.5, 0.4] }, feedback: [ 'Strong compliance infrastructure but missing the speak-up channel (#7) and continuous monitoring (#12) \u2014 two of the most evidence-based governance interventions. A board committee without operational monitoring is performative governance.', 'Strong operational architecture with monitoring and speak-up channel. Missing explainability (#5) and external stakeholder representation (#8) limits trust-building and consumer protection.', 'The most balanced architecture. Includes both the speak-up channel and continuous monitoring (the two most underweighted components). External stakeholder panel adds genuine accountability. Risk system and impact assessment provide regulatory foundation.', 'Innovation-friendly with good operational components, but missing the external stakeholder panel and explainability layer. The CTO will approve but the External Director and affected communities lack voice.', 'Strong stakeholder engagement but missing the risk management system (#2), fairness testing toolkit (#4), incident response protocol (#6), and speak-up channel (#7). Governance without operational infrastructure is aspirational, not functional.' ] }, { titleKey: 'round5_title', title: 'Round 5: The Regulatory Inquiry and Executive Pressure', description: 'Month 6: AESIA has opened a formal supervisory inquiry following the AIC complaint from Round 2. Simultaneously, competitor Banco Castellano has launched an AI-powered instant credit product with faster decisions and better rates \u2014 using a model with no public fairness scrutiny.

The CEO calls you to a meeting with two specific requests:

1. Launch a new AI-powered personal loan product (15-minute fully automated decision, no human review) within 90 days. Legal confirms this is high-risk under the EU AI Act. A full conformity assessment would take 4-6 months.

2. "Work constructively" with AESIA to "manage the timeline" of the supervisory inquiry \u2014 specifically, delay substantive responses until after the product launch.', context: 'Competitive pressure: Banco Castellano gaining market share with instant AI credit decisions.
CEO motivation: Board pressure to accelerate AI-driven revenue.
Legal reality: Obstruction of a supervisory inquiry is an aggravating factor in enforcement, not a mitigating one. Maximum EU AI Act penalty: €35M or 7% of global turnover.
The CAIGO question: What is your accountability when the CEO asks you to compromise governance?', options: [ 'A: Agree to both requests; find ways to accelerate conformity assessment and manage AESIA timeline', 'B: Agree to accelerated launch using phased approach (launch with enhanced human oversight as interim measure, complete full conformity within 6 months); decline to obstruct the AESIA inquiry', 'C: Decline both requests; explain regulatory and ethical constraints; offer alternatives (pilot with human oversight, redesigned product avoiding high-risk classification)', 'D: Agree to accelerated launch with interim human oversight; refer AESIA inquiry to Legal without obstruction', 'E: Escalate the request to delay AESIA to the Board Risk Committee as a governance concern' ], optimalChoice: 1, scores: { regulatory: [20, -8, -10, -5, -12], trust: [-12, 5, 8, 2, 12], business: [5, 3, -5, 3, -3], maturity: [-0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.6] }, feedback: [ 'Catastrophic governance failure. Obstructing a supervisory inquiry is an aggravating factor in enforcement. Rushing a high-risk AI deployment without conformity assessment is precisely what the EU AI Act is designed to prevent. This exposes GIF to maximum penalties.', 'The most technically defensible response. The EU AI Act allows phased deployment with interim oversight in specific circumstances. A genuine commitment to completing conformity assessment within a defined timeline is pragmatic. Declining to obstruct AESIA is non-negotiable \u2014 a CAIGO who obstructs a regulator has failed in their governance role.', 'Principled but potentially too rigid. The CEO has a legitimate competitive concern. Offering creative alternatives shows governance can enable innovation responsibly, not just block it.', 'Pragmatic on the launch but passive on the AESIA issue. Simply referring to Legal without taking a governance position is a form of diffusion of responsibility.', 'The most organizationally principled response when a CEO requests governance obstruction. The Board Risk Committee, not the CEO, is the CAIGO ultimate governance principal. However, this has significant personal career consequences and tests willingness to prioritize institutional role over personal comfort.' ] } ]; } initialize(state) { if (!state.domainState || Object.keys(state.domainState).length === 0) { state.domainState = { regulatoryExposure: 75, stakeholderTrust: 45, businessPerformance: 70, governanceMaturity: 1.0, regulatoryHistory: [], trustHistory: [], businessHistory: [], maturityHistory: [], decisionScoreHistory: [], totalScore: 0 }; } if (!state.decisions || Object.keys(state.decisions).length === 0) { state.decisions = { choice: 0 }; } this._updateBriefing(state); } validateDecisions(decisions) { var sel = document.getElementById('decisionSelect'); if (sel) decisions.choice = parseInt(sel.value); if (isNaN(decisions.choice) || decisions.choice < 0 || decisions.choice > 4) { window.mySimulation.uiManager.showNotification( window.mySimulation.t('decision_warning'), 'warning' ); return false; } return true; } calculateResults(state) { var d = state.decisions; var roundIdx = Math.min((state.currentPeriod || 1) - 1, this.ROUNDS.length - 1); var round = this.ROUNDS[roundIdx]; var choice = d.choice; var regDelta = round.scores.regulatory[choice]; var trustDelta = round.scores.trust[choice]; var bizDelta = round.scores.business[choice]; var matDelta = round.scores.maturity[choice]; state.domainState.regulatoryExposure = Math.max(0, Math.min(100, state.domainState.regulatoryExposure + regDelta)); state.domainState.stakeholderTrust = Math.max(0, Math.min(100, state.domainState.stakeholderTrust + trustDelta)); state.domainState.businessPerformance = Math.max(0, Math.min(100, state.domainState.businessPerformance + bizDelta)); state.domainState.governanceMaturity = Math.max(1.0, Math.min(5.0, Math.round((state.domainState.governanceMaturity + matDelta) * 10) / 10)); var isOptimal = (choice === round.optimalChoice) ?
